data: Surface pressure 90× Earth's. Soviet Venera probes lasted 23–127 minutes before the heat and pressure overwhelmed them.
Rotates retrograde — backwards and so slowly that a Venusian day is longer than its year. The 177.4° axial tilt is why: Venus is essentially upside down.
Venera 1–16 — USSR, 1961–83 (sustained Venus campaign; Venera 7 first soft-landing on another planet 1970; Venera 9 first surface images 1975)
Mariner 2 — NASA, 1962 (first successful interplanetary flyby of any planet)
Pioneer Venus 1 + 2 — NASA, 1978 (orbiter + multi-probe atmospheric descent)
Vega 1 + 2 — USSR, 1985 (lander + balloon, en route to Halley)
Magellan — NASA, 1990–94 (radar mapping of 98 % of the surface)
Venus Express — ESA, 2006–14 (polar orbit; super-rotation, lightning, atmospheric escape)
Akatsuki — JAXA, 2015– (equatorial cloud dynamics, currently active)
Parker Solar Probe + BepiColombo — multiple gravity-assist flybys (2020s)
Venus rotates retrograde with an axial tilt of 177° — effectively upside-down. Combined with a 243-day sidereal rotation, its day is longer than its 225-day year.
The most circular planetary orbit in the system (e = 0.0068) — Venus moves around the Sun like a near-perfect ring.
Venus has the most extreme greenhouse: surface temperatures stay ~460°C day and night, so the sub-solar / terminator distinction matters less than for any other planet.
Akatsuki (JAXA, 2015–) is the only active Venus orbiter; the Soviet Venera campaign (1961–83) still owns the only surface images ever taken.
Why Earth has seasons, why Uranus rolled onto its side, and why Venus spins backward.
How stretched the orbit is — zero is a perfect circle, one is a parabolic escape.
